title: Ear Disease, Hearing Loss and Vertigo
summary: Learn the key infections, hearing disorders and inner ear causes of dizziness.

lessons.title: Otitis Externa and Necrotizing Otitis Externa

levels.kid:
Your ear has a little tunnel that leads to your eardrum. It is called the **ear canal**. It has a waxy coat that keeps germs out, like a raincoat.

If water sits in the tunnel too long, like after lots of swimming, the raincoat gets soggy. Germs can sneak in and make the skin red, swollen and sore. This is called **swimmer's ear**. It hurts a lot when someone gently pulls your ear.

Doctors clean the ear and give special ear drops that kill the germs. Most kids feel better in a few days.

In some older people with sugar diabetes, the germs can dig deeper into the bone near the ear. That is rare and serious, so doctors treat it fast in the hospital.
levels.hs:
**Otitis externa** means inflammation of the outer ear canal, the skin-lined tube between the outer ear and the eardrum. It is usually a bacterial infection, and it is often called **swimmer's ear** because moisture is a major trigger.

The canal normally protects itself. **Cerumen** (earwax) is slightly acidic and water-repellent, which discourages bacterial growth. Problems start when this barrier breaks down:
- Water softens the skin and washes away wax
- Cotton swabs or fingernails scratch the skin
- Hearing aids or earbuds trap moisture
- Skin conditions such as eczema

The most common bacteria are ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa*** and ***Staphylococcus aureus***. Symptoms include ear pain, itching, discharge and muffled hearing. A classic sign is pain when the outer ear (the **pinna**) is pulled or the small flap in front of the canal (the **tragus**) is pressed. This helps tell it apart from a middle ear infection, where pulling the ear usually doesn't hurt.

Treatment is mainly **topical antibiotic ear drops**, often combined with a steroid to reduce swelling, plus keeping the ear dry. Pills are rarely needed.

A dangerous form, **necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa**, happens mostly in older adults with diabetes. The infection spreads into the bone of the skull base and needs urgent hospital care.
levels.college:
**Acute otitis externa (AOE)** is diffuse inflammation of the external auditory canal, usually bacterial. The lateral third of the canal is cartilaginous and hair-bearing with cerumen glands; the medial two-thirds is bony with thin skin tightly bound to periosteum, which is why swelling there is so painful.

**Pathogenesis.** Cerumen maintains an acidic pH (roughly 5-6) and a hydrophobic lipid layer. Moisture, maceration, trauma (cotton swabs, scratching) and occlusion (hearing aids) raise pH and disrupt the epithelium, allowing invasion.

**Microbiology.**
- *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Staphylococcus aureus* cause most cases, often together
- **Otomycosis** (fungal) is caused by *Aspergillus* (black or grey debris) or *Candida* (white), especially after prolonged antibiotic drops

**Clinical features.** Otalgia, often out of proportion to appearance, with tragal tenderness and pain on pinna traction; itching, discharge, aural fullness and conductive hearing loss from canal edema. The canal looks red and swollen with debris.

**Management.**
- **Aural toilet**: removing debris so drops can reach the skin
- Topical drops: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin), often with a corticosteroid; acidifying agents such as acetic acid
- A **wick** if the canal is too swollen for drops to enter
- Avoid ototoxic aminoglycoside drops if the tympanic membrane may be perforated
- Systemic antibiotics are reserved for spread beyond the canal or immunocompromise

**Necrotizing otitis externa (NOE)** is invasive infection spreading from the canal into the temporal bone and skull base, i.e. osteomyelitis. It classically affects elderly diabetics; *P. aeruginosa* causes the large majority. Warning signs are severe, persistent pain (often worse at night), **granulation tissue on the floor of the canal at the bony-cartilaginous junction**, and failure of topical therapy. Spread can involve cranial nerves, most commonly the **facial nerve (CN VII)** at the stylomastoid foramen.
levels.phd:
NOE pathogenesis reflects host and anatomic factors. In diabetes, microangiopathy reduces tissue perfusion, and hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis and killing. The **fissures of Santorini**, small defects in the cartilaginous canal floor, and the osseocartilaginous junction give a route inferiorly into the soft tissues below the temporal bone. From there infection tracks along the skull base to the stylomastoid foramen (CN VII), the jugular foramen (CN IX, X, XI), the hypoglossal canal (CN XII), and medially toward the petrous apex (CN V, VI) and the sigmoid sinus.

**Microbiology.** *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* is classic. Its virulence factors (elastase, alkaline protease, exotoxin A, biofilm formation) cause necrotizing vasculitis and tissue destruction. *S. aureus* including MRSA, and fungi (*Aspergillus*, especially in patients with neutropenia or HIV) are increasingly reported. Ciprofloxacin-resistant *Pseudomonas* is a growing problem, partly from widespread empirical fluoroquinolone use.

**Diagnosis.** No single test is definitive; diagnosis integrates clinical, laboratory and imaging findings.
- ESR and CRP are typically raised and are useful for following response, while white cell counts may be normal
- **CT** shows bony erosion but needs substantial demineralization (roughly 30-50% bone loss) before changes appear, and bone changes lag behind healing
- **MRI** better shows soft tissue, marrow and intracranial spread
- Nuclear imaging: technetium-99m bone scan is sensitive early but stays positive long after cure; gallium-67 or, increasingly, FDG-PET/CT track active inflammation and help decide when to stop treatment
- Biopsy of granulation tissue excludes **squamous cell carcinoma** of the canal, which can look identical, and provides culture

**Treatment.** Prolonged culture-guided systemic antipseudomonal therapy (e.g. ciprofloxacin, or ceftazidime/piperacillin-tazobactam IV), usually for at least 6 weeks, plus strict glycemic control. Surgery is limited to debridement and biopsy. Historic mortality exceeded 50% before antipseudomonal agents. Cranial neuropathy carries a worse prognosis, though whether facial palsy alone predicts mortality is debated.
levels.expert:
Clinical pearls and pitfalls center on recognition. The typical NOE patient has been given several courses of drops for "otitis externa that won't settle" before anyone notices that the pain is far greater than the canal appearance suggests. Any diabetic or immunosuppressed patient with persistent otalgia, nocturnal pain or canal floor granulation should have inflammatory markers and cross-sectional imaging, plus biopsy and culture before antibiotics where feasible. Cultures taken after topical fluoroquinolones may be falsely negative or select resistant organisms.

Other patients now recognized as at risk include those on chemotherapy, transplant recipients, people with HIV, and those with chronic kidney disease. Rare pediatric cases occur, often with leukemia or neutropenia.

**Mimics** include canal squamous cell carcinoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma with skull base invasion, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis. A lower cranial nerve palsy with skull base enhancement in an older patient raises both NOE and malignancy, so repeat biopsy is warranted if the course is atypical.

Definitions are not standardized. A 2022 international Delphi consensus (Hopkins and colleagues) proposed core diagnostic criteria (pain, a risk factor, compatible imaging) to make studies comparable, but trial evidence remains thin: duration of therapy, oral versus IV routes, and stopping rules are largely based on case series. Adjuncts such as hyperbaric oxygen are used inconsistently, with weak evidence.

For uncomplicated AOE, guidelines (AAO-HNS 2014) emphasize: treat with topical rather than oral antibiotics, assess pain and use analgesia, consider non-ototoxic drops when the eardrum is not intact, and reassess if not improving within 48-72 hours. Oral antibiotics are overprescribed and promote resistance.

Open questions: how best to monitor treatment response (serial CRP versus PET/CT or MRI diffusion), predictors of relapse (which can occur months later), and the role of rising antifungal and antimicrobial resistance. For a future neurosurgeon, NOE is a reminder that a "minor" ear problem can become skull base osteomyelitis complicated by venous sinus thrombosis or intracranial spread.

keyPoints: Otitis externa is infection of the ear canal, often triggered by moisture or trauma
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus are the main causes
Tragal tenderness and pain on pinna pulling are classic signs
Uncomplicated cases are treated with topical drops, cleaning and keeping dry
Necrotizing otitis externa is skull base osteomyelitis, mostly in elderly diabetics
Canal floor granulation, severe night pain and CN VII palsy are red flags

test.q: Which bacterium is the most common cause of otitis externa?
test.explain: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, often with Staphylococcus aureus, causes most cases. The other options are classic middle ear pathogens.

test.q: Which exam finding best suggests otitis externa rather than a middle ear infection?
test.explain: Pain on pinna traction or tragal pressure reflects inflamed canal skin. The other findings point to the middle ear.

test.q: How does earwax help protect the ear canal?
choices: It holds antibodies from the blood
It is acidic and repels water
It is alkaline and absorbs water
test.explain: Cerumen keeps the canal acidic and hydrophobic, discouraging bacterial growth.

test.q: What is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated otitis externa?
test.explain: Topical drops reach high local concentrations; oral antibiotics are reserved for spread or immunocompromise.

test.q: Why might a wick be placed in the ear canal?
choices: To hold the eardrum in its place
To drain pus from the middle ear
To let drops pass a swollen canal
test.explain: When the canal is too swollen for drops to enter, a wick carries medication inward.

test.q: Who is at highest risk of necrotizing otitis externa?
test.explain: Diabetic microangiopathy and impaired neutrophil function make elderly diabetics the classic group.

test.q: Necrotizing otitis externa is essentially an infection of which tissue?
test.explain: It is osteomyelitis spreading from the canal into the temporal bone and skull base.

test.q: Which cranial nerve is most commonly affected in necrotizing otitis externa?
test.explain: The facial nerve exits at the stylomastoid foramen, close to the spreading infection.

test.q: Black or grey debris in an itchy ear canal after long antibiotic drop use suggests:
test.explain: Aspergillus otomycosis typically shows black or grey debris; Candida tends to look white.

test.q: Otitis externa is commonly called ___ ear because moisture is a major trigger.
test.explain: Prolonged water exposure softens canal skin and washes away protective wax.

test.q: What is the medical name for earwax?
test.explain: Cerumen is the acidic, waxy secretion that protects the canal.

test.q: Fungal infection of the ear canal is called ___.
test.explain: Otomycosis is usually caused by Aspergillus or Candida.

kidTest.q: What is the ear canal?
kidTest.explain: The ear canal is the tunnel leading to your eardrum.

kidTest.q: What often causes swimmer's ear?
kidTest.explain: Water makes the skin soggy so germs can get in.

kidTest.q: What does earwax do?
choices: Keeps germs out of the ear
kidTest.explain: Earwax works like a raincoat that keeps germs out.

kidTest.q: How do doctors usually treat swimmer's ear?
choices: With a cast on the ear
kidTest.explain: Ear drops kill the germs in the canal.

kidTest.q: Swimmer's ear makes it hurt when someone gently pulls your ear. The ear gets red and s _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Infected skin in the canal becomes red, swollen and sore.

advancedTest.q: A diabetic man has had otitis externa for 6 weeks despite drops; his CT is normal but CRP is high. Best interpretation?
choices: A high CRP points to fungal infection, so switch to antifungals
CT excludes necrotizing otitis externa, so continue the drops
A normal CT suggests carcinoma, so arrange a skull base resection
CT changes need major bone loss, so get MRI and biopsy
advancedTest.explain: CT detects erosion only after roughly 30-50% demineralization, so early NOE can look normal. MRI and biopsy assess spread and exclude carcinoma.

advancedTest.q: Why is a technetium-99m bone scan poor for deciding when to stop NOE treatment?
choices: It misses early bone involvement in most patients
It blurs the canal together with the middle ear
It is falsely negative in patients with diabetes
It stays positive long after the infection is cured
advancedTest.explain: Bone remodeling keeps technetium scans positive after cure; gallium or FDG-PET better track active inflammation.

advancedTest.q: Granulation at the canal floor in a patient whose NOE fails to respond to antipseudomonal therapy most strongly warrants:
choices: Starting a second topical fluoroquinolone drop
Repeat biopsy for carcinoma and fungal culture
Stopping antibiotics to allow natural healing
Adding steroid drops to shrink the granulation
advancedTest.explain: Squamous cell carcinoma and fungal infection can mimic or complicate NOE, so tissue diagnosis is needed when the course is atypical.

advancedTest.q: Why should cultures ideally be taken before starting a topical fluoroquinolone in suspected NOE?
choices: Prior drops can give falsely negative cultures or select resistance
Fluoroquinolones turn Pseudomonas into Staphylococcus strains
Drops raise canal pH and favor fungal overgrowth
Drops destroy the cartilage needed for biopsy
advancedTest.explain: Prior topical antibiotics can suppress growth in cultures and select resistant organisms, undermining culture-guided long-term therapy.

lessons.title: Acute Otitis Media, Effusion and Cholesteatoma

levels.kid:
Behind your eardrum is a tiny room filled with air. It is called the **middle ear**. A little tube connects it to the back of your nose, like a pipe that lets air in and fluid drain out.

When you have a cold, that pipe can get blocked. Fluid gets stuck in the little room. Germs can grow there and make it sore. That is an **ear infection**. It can hurt a lot and give you a fever.

Sometimes the fluid stays even after the pain goes away. Then sounds seem muffled, like hearing underwater.

Very rarely, skin grows into the wrong place inside the ear and makes a lump that keeps growing. Doctors call it a **cholesteatoma**, and they fix it with an operation.
levels.hs:
The **middle ear** is an air-filled space behind the eardrum (tympanic membrane) that holds three tiny bones, the ossicles. It stays ventilated through the **Eustachian tube**, which runs to the back of the nose (nasopharynx).

**Acute otitis media (AOM)** is a sudden infection of the middle ear. It is most common in children aged 6 to 24 months because their Eustachian tubes are short, floppy and more horizontal. A cold swells the tube shut, fluid collects, and bacteria such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Moraxella catarrhalis* multiply. Signs include ear pain, fever, irritability and a **bulging, red eardrum**. Many cases improve without treatment. Doctors either prescribe antibiotics (amoxicillin is the usual first choice) or watch carefully for a couple of days.

**Otitis media with effusion (OME)**, sometimes called glue ear, is fluid in the middle ear *without* signs of infection. It often follows AOM and causes muffled hearing. If it lasts a long time and affects hearing or speech, surgeons may place **ear tubes** (tympanostomy tubes) to let air in.

**Cholesteatoma** is a growth of skin cells (keratinizing squamous epithelium) in the middle ear. It slowly erodes bone and can cause a smelly, persistent discharge and hearing loss. It needs surgery.

Example: a 1-year-old pulls at her ear, has a fever after a cold, and the doctor sees a bulging eardrum. That is AOM.
levels.college:
**Pathophysiology.** Eustachian tube dysfunction is the common thread. Viral upper respiratory infection causes tubal mucosal edema, negative middle-ear pressure, and transudation of fluid. Nasopharyngeal bacteria then reflux in and colonize that fluid. Several factors raise risk in infants: a shorter, more horizontal tube, a less efficient tensor veli palatini, adenoid hypertrophy, daycare exposure, bottle-feeding while lying flat, and passive smoke. Cleft palate is also a strong risk because the tensor veli palatini works poorly.

**AOM diagnosis** requires middle-ear effusion plus acute inflammation. The most specific sign is a **moderately to severely bulging tympanic membrane**. Redness alone is unreliable, because crying also reddens the drum. **Pneumatic otoscopy** shows reduced drum mobility.
- Pathogens: *S. pneumoniae*, nontypeable *H. influenzae* and *M. catarrhalis*. Respiratory viruses often coexist with them.
- Management (AAP 2013): give pain relief in every case. Antibiotics are advised for children under 6 months, severe disease and bilateral AOM under 2 years. Otherwise doctors may observe for 48 to 72 hours.
- Amoxicillin is first-line. Amoxicillin-clavulanate covers β-lactamase-producing *H. influenzae* and *Moraxella*.

**OME** is effusion without acute inflammation. The drum looks dull or retracted, sometimes with an air-fluid level, and the effusion causes a conductive hearing loss. Tympanometry shows a flat (type B) curve. Most cases clear within 3 months. Tubes are considered for effusion lasting 3 months or more with hearing loss, or in at-risk children. An adult with one-sided OME needs a nasopharyngeal exam to exclude a tumor blocking the tube.

**Cholesteatoma** is keratinizing squamous epithelium trapped in the middle ear or mastoid.
- **Acquired** (most common): a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida (attic) fills with keratin debris.
- **Congenital**: a white pearl behind an intact drum.
- It causes painless foul otorrhea and conductive loss, and it erodes the ossicles. Treatment is surgical: tympanomastoidectomy.

**Complications** of middle-ear disease include tympanic membrane perforation, mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, and intracranial spread such as meningitis, brain abscess and sigmoid sinus thrombosis.
levels.phd:
**Microbiology and vaccines.** Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV7 in 2000, PCV13 in 2010) reduced vaccine-serotype AOM. However, **serotype replacement** occurred, with serotype 19A emerging before PCV13 covered it. The share of nontypeable *H. influenzae* (NTHi) also rose, making it a co-dominant pathogen. NTHi and *M. catarrhalis* often produce β-lactamase, which protects not only themselves but also nearby pneumococci (indirect pathogenicity). Pneumococcal resistance comes from altered **penicillin-binding proteins**, not β-lactamase. That is why high-concentration amoxicillin overcomes it, while clavulanate addresses the Gram-negative organisms.

**Biofilms.** Post and colleagues detected bacterial DNA by PCR in many "sterile" culture-negative chronic effusions. Later work showed mucosal biofilms of NTHi in children with recurrent AOM and OME. Biofilms explain persistence, culture negativity and antibiotic tolerance. They also help explain why adenoidectomy, which removes a biofilm reservoir, reduces recurrence in some children.

**Effusion biology.** Chronic OME involves goblet cell metaplasia and upregulation of mucins, especially **MUC5B**. Inflammatory mediators drive this, including TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-8. The result is the viscous "glue." Gas exchange across the mucosa, which absorbs nitrogen, maintains negative pressure when the tube fails.

**Evidence on antibiotics.** Placebo-controlled trials (Hoberman 2011, Tähtinen 2011) used stringent diagnostic criteria. Under those criteria, amoxicillin-clavulanate reduced treatment failure compared with placebo in young children. Cochrane analyses across broader populations show modest absolute benefit: many children need treatment for one to gain pain relief by days 2 to 7. There is also a real burden of diarrhea and rash. The debate centers on diagnostic precision and on identifying subgroups such as under-2 bilateral disease and otorrhea.

**Cholesteatoma pathogenesis** has several competing theories:
- Invagination of a retraction pocket (Wittmaack).
- Migration of epithelium through a perforation (Habermann).
- Squamous metaplasia.
- Basal cell hyperplasia.
- Epidermoid rests explain congenital disease (Michaels).

Bone erosion is enzymatic and inflammatory rather than just pressure. Perimatrix fibroblasts and keratinocytes release RANKL, MMP-2/9 and cytokines that activate osteoclasts.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic pitfalls.** Primary-care diagnosis of AOM is notoriously inaccurate. Cerumen, crying-induced erythema and poor views drive overdiagnosis. The AAP 2013 guideline counters this by anchoring diagnosis on bulging rather than redness, plus new-onset otorrhea not caused by otitis externa. Tympanostomy tubes are indicated for recurrent AOM only when an effusion is present at assessment: 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 in 12 months, with one in the last 6 months. Hoberman's 2021 NEJM trial compared tubes with medical management for recurrent AOM. It found no significant reduction in episode rate, which has tempered enthusiasm. For OME, the 2016 AAO-HNS guideline recommends watchful waiting for at least 3 months. It recommends against intranasal or systemic steroids, antihistamines and decongestants, because trials show no durable benefit. Autoinflation devices have modest support.

**Tube otorrhea** is treated with topical quinolone drops, which are non-ototoxic, rather than oral antibiotics. Aminoglycoside drops are avoided when the drum is open.

**Cholesteatoma surgery and imaging.** Canal-wall-up mastoidectomy preserves anatomy but leaves residual or recurrent disease in a meaningful minority. Classically this required a planned "second look" at 9 to 12 months. **Non-EPI diffusion-weighted MRI**, such as HASTE-DWI, now detects residual keratin of a few millimetres. Keratin restricts diffusion, which granulation tissue does not, so DWI MRI has largely replaced routine second-look surgery. Canal-wall-down procedures lower recurrence but create a cavity that needs lifelong cleaning. Endoscopic ear surgery improves visualization of hidden recesses such as the sinus tympani and facial recess, the classic sites of residual disease. High-resolution CT maps erosion of the tegmen, lateral semicircular canal (fistula) and fallopian canal before surgery.

**Neurosurgical interface.** Otogenic intracranial complications include temporal lobe and cerebellar abscess, subdural empyema, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and otitic hydrocephalus. These require combined otologic and neurosurgical management. Gradenigo syndrome is petrous apicitis producing otorrhea, abducens palsy and trigeminal pain.

**Open questions.** Several areas remain unresolved:
- Whether to add an NTHi-protein-D-based or broader-valency pneumococcal vaccine (PCV15/20).
- Antibiotic-free management, using smartphone otoscopy and AI-assisted drum classification.
- Anti-biofilm strategies.
- Molecular targeting of cholesteatoma's keratinocyte hyperproliferation (EGFR, RANKL).

keyPoints: Eustachian tube dysfunction underlies acute otitis media and effusion
AOM pathogens: S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis
A bulging eardrum is the most specific sign of AOM; redness alone is unreliable
OME is fluid without infection, causes conductive loss, and gives a flat tympogram
Cholesteatoma is trapped keratinizing epithelium that erodes bone and needs surgery
Complications include mastoiditis, facial palsy and intracranial infection

test.q: Which structure ventilates the middle ear and connects it to the nasopharynx?
test.explain: The Eustachian tube equalizes pressure and drains the middle ear. When it is blocked, fluid builds up.

test.q: Which otoscopic finding is most specific for acute otitis media?
test.explain: Bulging indicates pus under pressure. Redness alone is unreliable because crying also reddens the drum.

test.q: Why are infants especially prone to otitis media?
choices: Their ossicles are not yet formed
Their ear canals are longer and narrower
Their Eustachian tubes are short and horizontal
test.explain: A short, floppy, horizontal tube drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal bacteria reflux into the middle ear.

test.q: Which organism is a classic bacterial cause of acute otitis media?
test.explain: The big three are S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis. Pseudomonas is typical of otitis externa.

test.q: How does otitis media with effusion differ from acute otitis media?
choices: Fluid is present without acute inflammation
It produces a high fever and severe pain
It is caused mainly by fungal infection
It affects the outer ear canal instead
test.explain: OME is middle-ear fluid without signs of acute infection. It often follows AOM and muffles hearing.

test.q: What tympanometry result is typical of a middle-ear effusion?
test.explain: Fluid stops the eardrum from moving, so the curve is flat (type B). Type C reflects negative pressure without fluid filling the space.

test.q: A cholesteatoma is best described as:
choices: A malignant tumor of the eardrum
A cholesterol deposit in the cochlea
A bacterial abscess of the mastoid bone
Trapped keratinizing skin in the middle ear
test.explain: Despite its name, it is not cholesterol or cancer. It is squamous epithelium that sheds keratin and erodes bone.

test.q: An adult has fluid behind one eardrum. Why examine the nasopharynx?
choices: To look for a blocking tumor
To look for a deviated septum
test.explain: A nasopharyngeal tumor can block the Eustachian tube and cause one-sided effusion in an adult.

test.q: Which antibiotic is the usual first-line choice for acute otitis media?
test.explain: Amoxicillin is first-line. Amoxicillin-clavulanate adds cover for β-lactamase producers.

test.q: Small tubes placed in the eardrum to ventilate the middle ear are called ___ tubes.
test.explain: Tympanostomy tubes (grommets) let air into the middle ear when the Eustachian tube fails.

test.q: What common name describes thick, long-lasting middle-ear effusion in children?
test.explain: The viscous mucoid effusion of chronic OME is called glue ear.

test.q: Infection spreading into the air cells behind the ear is called ___.
test.explain: Mastoiditis is a classic complication of middle-ear infection.

kidTest.q: Where is the little air room that gets infected?
kidTest.explain: The middle ear sits behind the eardrum.

kidTest.q: What often comes just before an ear infection?
kidTest.explain: A cold can block the tube and trap fluid.

kidTest.q: How can sounds seem when fluid stays in the ear?
kidTest.explain: Fluid makes hearing sound muffled, like being underwater.

kidTest.q: How do doctors fix a cholesteatoma?
kidTest.explain: It is a growing lump of skin, so it needs surgery.

kidTest.q: The thin skin you hear with is the ear d _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear.

advancedTest.q: Why does adding clavulanate help in AOM but not against resistant pneumococci?
choices: Clavulanate mainly blocks efflux pumps in Gram-positives
Pneumococci resist via altered PBPs, not β-lactamase
Clavulanate reaches middle-ear fluid at too low a level
advancedTest.explain: Clavulanate inhibits β-lactamase made by NTHi and Moraxella. Pneumococcal resistance comes from altered penicillin-binding proteins, which higher amoxicillin levels overcome.

advancedTest.q: Culture-negative chronic effusions often contain bacterial DNA. The best explanation is:
choices: Viral infection that leaves bacterial DNA behind
Contamination from the ear canal during sampling
Mucosal biofilms with bacteria that culture poorly
Sterile inflammation from an allergic reaction
advancedTest.explain: Biofilm-embedded bacteria, especially NTHi, persist with low growth rates. They are culture-negative but PCR-positive and tolerant of antibiotics.

advancedTest.q: Why has diffusion-weighted MRI largely replaced planned second-look surgery after cholesteatoma removal?
choices: Keratin restricts diffusion, while granulation tissue does not
MRI shows ossicular erosion better than CT does
Diffusion imaging measures how well the ossicles conduct sound
Keratin enhances strongly with gadolinium contrast
advancedTest.explain: Non-EPI DWI exploits restricted diffusion in keratin to detect small residual disease and separate it from scar or granulation tissue.

advancedTest.q: After pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, the share of AOM caused by NTHi rose. This reflects:
choices: Vaccine-induced antibodies cross-reacting with H. influenzae
A rise in middle-ear β-lactamase from vaccine adjuvants
Better culture methods introduced at the same time
Microbial niche replacement after removing vaccine serotypes
advancedTest.explain: Removing vaccine serotypes from the nasopharynx opened the niche to non-vaccine pneumococci and NTHi. This is serotype and species replacement.

lessons.title: Conductive vs Sensorineural Hearing Loss and Sudden Hearing Loss

levels.kid:
Your ear is like a relay race. First, sound waves travel down the ear tube and shake your eardrum. Tiny bones pass the shake along. Then, deep inside, a snail-shaped part called the **cochlea** turns the shake into nerve signals for your brain.

If something blocks the first part, like earwax or fluid, sound can't get through well. Doctors call that **conductive** hearing loss. It is often fixable.

If the cochlea or the hearing nerve is hurt, the signal gets lost. That is **sensorineural** hearing loss.

Sometimes a person suddenly can't hear well in one ear, like someone turned the volume down overnight. That is an emergency for ears! Seeing a doctor fast gives the best chance of getting hearing back.
levels.hs:
Hearing has two big stages. The **outer and middle ear** carry sound mechanically: the ear canal funnels sound to the eardrum, and three tiny bones (the **ossicles**: malleus, incus, stapes) pass vibrations to the inner ear. The **inner ear** (cochlea) contains **hair cells** that convert vibration into electrical signals sent along the **cochlear nerve** to the brain.

- **Conductive hearing loss (CHL)**: a problem getting sound to the inner ear. Causes include earwax, ear infections with fluid, a hole in the eardrum, or stiff ossicles (**otosclerosis**).
- **Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)**: damage to the cochlea or nerve. Causes include aging (**presbycusis**), loud noise, some medicines, and rarely tumors of the nerve.
- **Mixed**: both at once.

Doctors tell them apart with a **tuning fork** and a hearing test called an **audiogram**. In the **Weber test**, a fork placed on the forehead sounds louder in the *bad* ear with conductive loss but in the *good* ear with sensorineural loss.

**Sudden sensorineural hearing loss** means losing a lot of hearing in one ear within 72 hours, often noticed on waking, sometimes with ringing or a full feeling. It is an urgent problem: doctors usually treat it quickly with **steroids**, because early treatment improves the chance of recovery. Example: a 45-year-old wakes up muffled in one ear with no wax or infection. A Weber test that sounds louder in the healthy ear points to sensorineural loss and needs urgent care.
levels.college:
**Anatomy of the defect.** Conductive loss arises anywhere from the external canal to the stapes footplate; sensorineural loss arises in the cochlea (sensory) or the cochlear nerve and central pathways (neural, or **retrocochlear**).

**Bedside tuning fork tests (512 Hz):**
- **Rinne**: compares air conduction (AC) with bone conduction (BC, fork on mastoid). Normally AC > BC ("Rinne positive"). With significant CHL, BC > AC ("Rinne negative"). In SNHL, AC > BC still, both reduced.
- **Weber**: fork on the midline skull. Lateralizes to the affected ear in CHL (the masking effect of ambient noise is lost) and to the better ear in SNHL.

**Audiometry.** Pure-tone audiometry plots thresholds in decibels hearing level (dB HL) across frequencies (about 250 to 8000 Hz). An **air-bone gap** (AC thresholds worse than BC by more than about 10 dB) indicates a conductive component; in SNHL, air and bone thresholds are equally elevated. **Tympanometry** assesses middle-ear compliance: a flat (type B) trace suggests effusion or perforation.

**Causes:**
- CHL: cerumen impaction, otitis media with effusion, tympanic membrane perforation, cholesteatoma, ossicular discontinuity, otosclerosis (fixed stapes; **Carhart notch** near 2 kHz on bone conduction).
- SNHL: presbycusis (bilateral, high-frequency), noise (notch near 4 kHz), ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, loop diuretics), infections (meningitis, congenital CMV), Ménière's disease, and **vestibular schwannoma**.

**Sudden SNHL (SSNHL)** is defined as a loss of at least 30 dB across three consecutive frequencies developing within 72 hours. Most cases are **idiopathic**. Workup: confirm sensorineural (exclude wax, effusion), audiogram, and **MRI with gadolinium** to exclude a retrocochlear lesion. Treatment is corticosteroids, oral or **intratympanic**, ideally within two weeks. Roughly a third to two-thirds recover some hearing, with many recoveries spontaneous.
levels.phd:
**Cochlear mechanics.** The middle ear compensates for the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch mainly through the area ratio of the tympanic membrane to the stapes footplate (about 17:1) plus ossicular lever action, giving roughly 25 to 30 dB of gain. This explains why complete ossicular discontinuity behind an intact drum can produce a conductive loss approaching 60 dB. The **outer hair cells** provide active amplification through the motor protein **prestin**, which changes cell length with voltage and sharpens frequency tuning; their function is measured by **otoacoustic emissions (OAEs)**. **Inner hair cells** are the true transducers, releasing glutamate at ribbon synapses onto type I spiral ganglion neurons.

**Hidden hearing loss.** Kujawa and Liberman (2009) showed that noise exposure causing only a temporary threshold shift in mice permanently destroyed a large fraction of inner hair cell ribbon synapses. This **cochlear synaptopathy** leaves audiogram thresholds normal yet degrades hearing in noise. Human evidence remains contested, partly because measures like the auditory brainstem response (ABR) wave I amplitude vary widely between people.

**Ototoxicity mechanisms.** Aminoglycosides enter hair cells via mechanotransduction channels and generate reactive oxygen species, killing basal (high-frequency) outer hair cells first. The mitochondrial **m.1555A>G** variant in *MT-RNR2*'s neighbour *MT-RNR1* (12S rRNA) makes the ribosome more bacterial-like and greatly increases susceptibility, even after brief exposure. Cisplatin is retained in the cochlea for months and acts partly through stria vascularis injury. **Sodium thiosulfate** was FDA-approved (Pedmark, 2022) to reduce cisplatin ototoxicity in children with localized solid tumors.

**SSNHL pathogenesis** is unresolved. Proposed mechanisms include viral cochleitis, microvascular occlusion of the labyrinthine artery (an end artery), immune-mediated injury and intracochlear membrane rupture. No single model explains the heterogeneity. Prognosis worsens with severe initial loss, vertigo, older age, delay to treatment and a downsloping configuration. Low-frequency losses do better. Randomized trials (Rauch et al., JAMA 2011) found intratympanic steroids noninferior to oral steroids as primary therapy; they are also used as salvage after oral treatment fails.
levels.expert:
**Clinical pitfalls.** The most consequential error is labelling unilateral sudden loss as "just fluid" or wax and prescribing decongestants. The 2019 AAO-HNS guideline urges clinicians to distinguish sensorineural from conductive loss at first presentation, using tuning forks if audiometry is unavailable, because the steroid window is time-sensitive. Rinne testing has limits: false-negative Rinne in a dead ear occurs because bone-conducted sound crosses the skull to the opposite cochlea. Proper audiometry uses **masking** to prevent this cross-hearing.

**Imaging and retrocochlear disease.** Vestibular schwannoma presents with SSNHL in a minority of cases, and hearing may even recover with steroids, so recovery does not exclude a tumour. MRI of the internal auditory canals with contrast (or high-resolution T2 sequences such as CISS/FIESTA for screening) is standard for asymmetric SNHL. Routine labs and CT are not recommended for idiopathic SSNHL without specific indications. Bilateral simultaneous sudden loss is atypical and should prompt a search for systemic causes: autoimmune disease, neoplasm, vascular events (anterior inferior cerebellar artery infarction can cause sudden deafness with vertigo), syphilis or meningitis.

**Adjuncts and controversies.** **Hyperbaric oxygen** is an option within 2 weeks of onset (or 1 month as salvage) per guideline, with modest supporting evidence. Antivirals, vasodilators and antioxidants are not recommended. Combined systemic plus intratympanic therapy remains debated.

**Rehabilitation.** Persistent single-sided deafness can be managed with CROS hearing aids, bone-anchored devices or, increasingly, **cochlear implantation**, which uniquely restores binaural input and often reduces tinnitus. Conductive losses are frequently surgically correctable: stapedotomy for otosclerosis, tympanoplasty and ossiculoplasty.

**Frontiers.** Gene therapy (AAV-delivered *OTOF*) restored hearing in children with otoferlin deafness in 2023-2024 trials, a landmark for hereditary SNHL. Drugs targeting hair-cell regeneration (Atoh1 pathways, Notch/Wnt modulation) and synaptopathy repair (neurotrophins like NT-3) are in development, though early regenerative trials disappointed. **Hearing loss and dementia**: the Lancet Commission lists midlife hearing loss as a leading modifiable risk factor, and the ACHIEVE trial (2023) suggested hearing intervention slowed cognitive decline in higher-risk older adults, a still-evolving area.

keyPoints: Conductive loss blocks sound before the inner ear; sensorineural loss damages cochlea or nerve
Weber lateralizes to the bad ear in conductive loss, to the good ear in sensorineural loss
Rinne: bone louder than air conduction signals conductive loss
An air-bone gap on the audiogram marks a conductive component
Sudden SNHL: 30 dB or more over 3 frequencies within 72 hours, an otologic emergency
Treat sudden SNHL with early steroids and get an MRI to exclude vestibular schwannoma

lessons.title: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo and Vestibular Neuritis

levels.kid:
Deep inside each ear is a tiny balance system. It has loops filled with liquid, a bit like the bubble in a builder's level. When your head turns, the liquid moves and tells your brain which way you went.

Sometimes tiny crystals, like grains of sand, slip into one of the loops. Then, when you roll over in bed, the room seems to spin for a few seconds. This is called **BPPV**. A doctor can fix it by gently turning your head in special steps so the crystals roll back home.

Other times a germ makes the balance nerve swell up. Then the spinning lasts for days, not seconds. Rest helps, and the brain slowly learns to balance again.
levels.hs:
**Vertigo** is the false feeling that you or the room is spinning. Two of the most common inner-ear causes are BPPV and vestibular neuritis.

The inner ear has three **semicircular canals** filled with fluid called **endolymph**. They sense head rotation. Two nearby sacs, the **utricle** and **saccule**, sense gravity using tiny calcium carbonate crystals called **otoconia**.

**Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV):**
- Otoconia break loose and drift into a canal, usually the **posterior canal**.
- Turning over in bed, looking up, or bending down triggers spinning that lasts **less than a minute**.
- Doctors confirm it with the **Dix-Hallpike test**. The patient's head is turned and lowered backward, which brings on brief vertigo and jerking eye movements called **nystagmus**.
- Treatment is the **Epley maneuver**, a series of head positions that rolls the crystals back into the utricle. It often works in one session.

**Vestibular neuritis:**
- Inflammation of the vestibular nerve, often after a viral illness.
- It causes sudden, severe, **constant** vertigo with nausea that lasts days. **Hearing is normal**.
- Recovery takes weeks as the brain compensates.

Example: a 55-year-old woman spins for 20 seconds every time she rolls onto her right side in bed. A positive right Dix-Hallpike test points to right posterior-canal BPPV.
levels.college:
Dizziness is easiest to sort by **timing and triggers**, not by the patient's descriptive words. BPPV and vestibular neuritis sit at opposite ends of this scheme.

**BPPV: brief, triggered episodes**
- Mechanism: otoconia detach from the utricular macula (after age-related degeneration, head trauma, or prolonged bed rest) and enter a semicircular canal. This is **canalithiasis**. Gravity pulls the debris through the canal when the head moves, so endolymph flows and the cupula is deflected.
- The **posterior canal** is affected in roughly 80-90% of cases because it is the most dependent canal when a person lies down or sits up.
- **Dix-Hallpike**: after a latency of a few seconds, there is **upbeating, torsional nystagmus** with the top pole of the eye beating toward the lower ear. It lasts under a minute and fatigues when the test is repeated.
- **Horizontal-canal BPPV** is diagnosed with the **supine roll test** and produces horizontal nystagmus that changes direction with head position.
- Treatment: canalith repositioning, either the **Epley** or the **Semont** maneuver for the posterior canal, and the **Lempert (barbecue) roll** for the horizontal canal. Vestibular-suppressant drugs are not recommended for BPPV.

**Vestibular neuritis: an acute vestibular syndrome**
- Presumed viral or post-viral inflammation (herpes simplex type 1 reactivation is suspected), usually of the **superior vestibular nerve**.
- Continuous vertigo, nausea, and gait unsteadiness last for days. **Spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus beats away from the affected side.** It gets stronger when the patient looks toward the fast phase (Alexander's law) and is suppressed by visual fixation.
- The **head impulse test** is positive toward the affected side: a corrective catch-up saccade appears.
- If hearing loss is also present, the condition is called **labyrinthitis**.
- Management: brief symptomatic treatment, early **vestibular rehabilitation**, and in some protocols corticosteroids.
levels.phd:
**Biophysics.** Each semicircular canal ends in an ampulla, where the gelatinous cupula spans the lumen. Normally the cupula has the same density as endolymph, so it responds only to angular acceleration. In **canalithiasis**, free otoconial debris (calcium carbonate on a glycoprotein matrix) sediments through the canal. It acts like a plunger and drives endolymph flow. This explains the classic features:
- **Latency**: the particles need a moment to start moving.
- **Crescendo-decrescendo course**: flow builds, then stops once the particles settle.
- **Fatigability**: the debris disperses on repeat testing.

In **cupulolithiasis**, debris sticks to the cupula and makes it gravity-sensitive. Nystagmus then persists as long as the head position is held. In horizontal-canal BPPV, this produces an **apogeotropic** pattern (beating away from the ground), whereas canalithiasis produces a **geotropic** pattern. Schuknecht proposed cupulolithiasis in 1969, and Hall and colleagues later described the free-floating canalith model.

**Nystagmus direction follows Ewald's laws** and the excitatory connections of each canal. When the posterior canal is excited, the ipsilateral superior oblique and contralateral inferior rectus contract. The slow phase is downward and torsional, so the quick phase beats upward and torsionally toward the lower ear.

**Vestibular neuritis.** Temporal bone studies show degeneration of the vestibular nerve and Scarpa's ganglion. Latent **HSV-1** has been found in vestibular ganglia, but direct proof of causation is lacking. The superior division (anterior and horizontal canals, utricle) is affected far more often than the inferior division (posterior canal, saccule). This may be because the superior division runs through a longer, narrower bony channel. As a result, the caloric test and video head impulse test (vHIT) gains are often reduced, while cervical VEMPs (a saccular, inferior-nerve reflex) are spared.

**Steroid controversy.** In a randomized trial, Strupp and colleagues (NEJM 2004) showed that methylprednisolone improved recovery of peripheral vestibular function, while valacyclovir did not help. However, later analyses, including a Cochrane review, found no clear improvement in long-term symptoms. Steroid use therefore remains debated.

**Compensation.** Recovery happens centrally. The brainstem rebalances the resting activity of the two vestibular nuclei, guided by the cerebellum. Vestibular-suppressant drugs slow this process if they are continued.
levels.expert:
**The stroke mimic problem.** A patient with acute, continuous vertigo and nystagmus may have vestibular neuritis or a posterior circulation stroke. Up to about 10-20% of such patients have a central cause, and early diffusion-weighted MRI misses many small brainstem and cerebellar infarcts in the first 24-48 hours. **HINTS** (Kattah et al., Stroke 2009) is more sensitive than early MRI when it is done by trained examiners:
- **Head Impulse**: a normal (negative) test in a patient with acute vertigo is *worrying*, because it suggests a central cause.
- **Nystagmus**: direction-changing on gaze testing suggests a central cause.
- **Test of Skew**: a vertical skew deviation suggests a central cause.

**HINTS-plus** adds new hearing loss, which can come from an AICA infarct affecting the labyrinth. A pitfall is applying HINTS to patients without continuous vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus: a normal head impulse test in a patient with episodic dizziness is meaningless. Severe truncal ataxia, meaning the patient cannot sit or stand unaided, also points to a central cause.

**BPPV pitfalls:**
- Pure downbeat or persistent positional nystagmus that does not fatigue suggests **central positional nystagmus** (for example, a cerebellar nodulus lesion or Chiari malformation). Anterior-canal BPPV is rare.
- Untreated BPPV raises fall risk in older adults, so screening in falls clinics is worthwhile.
- Recurrence is common, around 15% per year in many series, and has been linked to low vitamin D. Supplementation reduced recurrence in a Korean randomized trial (Jeong et al., Neurology 2020).
- Post-traumatic BPPV is often bilateral or involves several canals. This is relevant after head injury and neurosurgical procedures.

**Advances.** Video-oculography and vHIT have made the examination objective. Mechanical repositioning chairs help in refractory or immobile patients. Canal plugging is a rare option for intractable posterior-canal BPPV.

**Open questions:**
- Why do about half of vestibular neuritis patients develop **persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD)** or anxiety-driven chronic symptoms despite good peripheral recovery?
- Psychological factors and visual dependence during the acute phase predict poor outcome better than the size of the canal deficit does.
- This suggests early rehabilitation and cognitive approaches are as important as anything aimed at the nerve itself.

keyPoints: BPPV: loose otoconia in a canal (usually posterior) cause brief positional vertigo
Dix-Hallpike diagnoses posterior-canal BPPV; Epley maneuver treats it
Vestibular neuritis: days of constant vertigo, normal hearing, likely viral
Neuritis nystagmus beats away from the lesion; head impulse test is abnormal
HINTS exam separates neuritis from posterior circulation stroke
Recovery from neuritis relies on central compensation and vestibular rehab

test.explain: The fast phase beats away from the affected side, so a right-sided lesion gives left-beating nystagmus.

test.explain: The superior division, serving the anterior and horizontal canals and utricle, is affected far more often.

test.explain: Epley or Semont repositioning moves the debris back to the utricle. Suppressant drugs are not recommended for BPPV.

test.explain: A failing vestibulo-ocular reflex lets the eyes drift with the head, so a catch-up saccade is needed toward the affected side.

test.explain: The Epley maneuver (or the Semont maneuver) repositions the otoconia.

test.explain: Otoconia normally sit on the utricular macula and sense gravity.

test.explain: Early vestibular rehabilitation speeds central compensation.

kidTest.explain: Fluid in the loops tells your brain how your head moves.

kidTest.q: In BPPV, what slips into a loop of the ear?
kidTest.explain: Tiny crystals, like sand, roll into the loop.

kidTest.q: How can a doctor fix BPPV?
kidTest.explain: Special head turns roll the crystals back home.

kidTest.explain: A swollen balance nerve causes spinning for days, not seconds.

They test the saccule via the spared inferior nerve

choices: Antivirals add a clear benefit to steroids

Steroids reliably prevent progression to PPPD

lessons.title: Ménière's Disease and Tinnitus

levels.kid:
Deep inside your ear is a tiny curly tube filled with special water. It helps you hear and keeps you balanced, like a spirit level that builders use.

In **Ménière's disease**, that tube gets too full of fluid, like a water balloon stretched tight. Then a person can have sudden spinning dizzy spells that last for hours. Their ear feels full, sounds get muffled, and they hear a ringing or roaring noise.

That noise is called **tinnitus**. Lots of people hear ringing after a loud concert. Usually it fades away. But sometimes it stays.

Doctors help by changing what people eat, giving medicines and teaching ways to make the ringing feel less bothersome. Protecting your ears from loud noise helps too!
levels.hs:
**Ménière's disease** is an inner ear disorder that causes repeated attacks of four classic symptoms:
- **Vertigo**: a spinning sensation lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours
- **Fluctuating hearing loss**, usually low-pitched at first
- **Tinnitus**: hearing a sound (often roaring) that has no outside source
- **Aural fullness**: a feeling of pressure in the ear

The inner ear contains a fluid called **endolymph**. In Ménière's, too much endolymph builds up, a condition called **endolymphatic hydrops**. Scientists still debate whether hydrops actually causes the attacks or is just a marker of the disease. Over years, hearing in the affected ear often gets permanently worse.

Treatment begins with lifestyle changes such as a low-salt diet and limiting caffeine, plus diuretics and medicines that calm vertigo during attacks. Severe cases may need injections into the middle ear or surgery.

**Tinnitus** is much more common than Ménière's. Roughly 10-15% of adults have it. Most cases come with some hearing loss, often from noise exposure or aging. Example: a musician who played loud gigs for years may notice constant high-pitched ringing along with trouble hearing high notes. Tinnitus heard in only one ear, or tinnitus that pulses with the heartbeat, needs a doctor's check because it can signal other problems.
levels.college:
**Ménière's disease (MD)** is defined clinically. The 2015 Bárány Society criteria for **definite MD** require:
- Two or more spontaneous vertigo episodes, each 20 minutes to 12 hours long
- Audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency **sensorineural hearing loss** in the affected ear, on at least one occasion before, during or after an episode
- Fluctuating aural symptoms (hearing, tinnitus, fullness) in that ear
- No better explanation for the symptoms

The histopathological hallmark is **endolymphatic hydrops**: distension of the scala media and saccule as endolymph accumulates. Endolymph is a high-potassium fluid made by the **stria vascularis** and absorbed partly by the **endolymphatic sac**. Rupture or potassium leak into perilymph was once thought to depolarize hair cells and trigger attacks, but this theory is unproven. Onset is typically at age 40-60. The disease affects both ears in up to roughly a third of patients over time.

The course often moves from fluctuating hearing loss to fixed, flat loss. Late **Tumarkin otolithic crises** (sudden drop attacks without loss of consciousness) can occur.

Management is stepwise:
- Low-sodium diet, plus avoiding caffeine and alcohol (weak evidence)
- Diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide; betahistine is widely used in Europe
- Vestibular suppressants such as meclizine or benzodiazepines, used for acute attacks only
- **Intratympanic corticosteroids**, which preserve hearing
- **Intratympanic gentamicin**, a chemical labyrinthectomy that ablates vestibular hair cells and carries some hearing risk
- Surgery: endolymphatic sac decompression, vestibular nerve section, or labyrinthectomy

**Tinnitus** is subjective (heard only by the patient) or rarely objective. Most subjective tinnitus accompanies sensorineural hearing loss. Red flags include unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss, which raises concern for **vestibular schwannoma** and calls for MRI. **Pulsatile tinnitus** suggests a vascular cause.
levels.phd:
Endolymphatic hydrops can be induced experimentally. Kimura's 1960s work showed that obliterating the endolymphatic duct and sac in guinea pigs reliably produces hydrops. Yet these animals rarely show episodic vertigo. Human temporal bone studies by Merchant, Adams and Nadol found hydrops in every MD case examined. They also found it in people who never had symptoms. They concluded that hydrops is a marker, not necessarily the cause. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI (intratympanic or delayed intravenous, 3T FLAIR) now shows hydrops in living patients. It also reveals a subset with asymptomatic contralateral hydrops.

Proposed causes are multifactorial:
- **Familial MD** in roughly 5-10% of cases, with variants reported in genes such as *DTNA*, *FAM136A*, *SEMA3D* and *DPT*
- Autoimmune and inflammatory associations (an allergic/type 2 subgroup)
- Overlap with **vestibular migraine**, which shares episodic vertigo and is frequently comorbid
- Abnormal ion transport involving aquaporin-2, which is vasopressin-regulated, together with sac dysfunction

The therapeutic logic follows the cell biology. Gentamicin is concentrated in vestibular type I hair cells more than cochlear cells. This allows titrated vestibular ablation, though some sensorineural loss remains a risk.

The **BEMED trial** (Adrion et al., BMJ 2016) found betahistine no better than placebo for attack frequency. This weakened the evidence for its widespread use.

Tinnitus is now modeled as a central phenomenon triggered by peripheral deafferentation. Reduced cochlear input causes compensatory **increased central gain** in the dorsal cochlear nucleus and inferior colliculus. It also produces tonotopic map reorganization and hyperactivity in auditory cortex. Limbic and attentional networks (amygdala, anterior cingulate, parahippocampal regions) determine distress, which explains why perceived loudness correlates poorly with suffering. **Cochlear synaptopathy** ('hidden hearing loss'), described by Kujawa and Liberman in 2009, is the loss of ribbon synapses after noise exposure despite normal thresholds. It may explain tinnitus in people with normal audiograms, though its relevance in humans is debated.
levels.expert:
Clinical pitfalls in MD start with overdiagnosis. Many patients labeled 'Ménière's' have vestibular migraine, which presents with episodic vertigo and sometimes fullness but rarely progressive low-frequency loss. Serial audiograms are essential, because a single normal test does not exclude MD. Always image asymmetric sensorineural loss with MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude vestibular schwannoma, which can mimic MD. Consider autoimmune inner ear disease when progression is bilateral and rapid. Electrocochleography (raised SP/AP ratio) and VEMP tuning shifts are supportive but have limited sensitivity.

Treatment choices hinge on hearing status:
- **Serviceable hearing**: favor hearing-sparing options such as intratympanic steroids, endolymphatic sac surgery, or vestibular nerve section
- **Non-serviceable hearing**: intratympanic gentamicin or labyrinthectomy, often paired with **cochlear implantation**, which now restores useful hearing after labyrinthectomy
- Pursue ablation with caution because bilateral disease can develop; bilateral vestibular loss causes oscillopsia and disabling imbalance
- Positive-pressure devices (Meniett) failed to show benefit in controlled trials

For tinnitus, the 2014 AAO-HNS guideline recommends an audiogram, hearing aids when hearing loss is present, and **cognitive behavioral therapy**, which has the strongest evidence for reducing distress. It recommends against routine antidepressants, anticonvulsants, ginkgo or dietary supplements for tinnitus itself. Sound therapy and tinnitus retraining therapy are options.

Work up **pulsatile tinnitus** with an exam (otoscopy for a retrotympanic mass such as a paraganglioma) and vascular imaging. Causes include:
- Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, which commonly presents with venous pulsatile tinnitus
- Sigmoid sinus diverticulum or dehiscence
- Dural arteriovenous fistula, which carries hemorrhage risk
- Carotid stenosis or dissection

Objective tinnitus can also arise from palatal or middle ear myoclonus.

Frontiers include bimodal neuromodulation. The Lenire device pairs sound with tongue stimulation, and Shore's group combined sound with somatosensory stimulation targeting the dorsal cochlear nucleus, with early trials showing reduced tinnitus. Inner ear drug delivery, gene therapy for hereditary deafness, and hydrops imaging as a trial endpoint are also being pursued. Whether reversing hydrops changes the natural history of MD remains unanswered.

keyPoints: Ménière's: episodic vertigo (20 min-12 h), fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
Hallmark pathology is endolymphatic hydrops, but it may be a marker rather than the cause
Stepwise treatment: low salt and diuretics, then intratympanic steroids or gentamicin, then surgery
Tinnitus is a phantom sound, usually linked to hearing loss and increased central gain
Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss needs MRI to exclude vestibular schwannoma
Pulsatile tinnitus suggests a vascular cause; CBT best reduces tinnitus distress

test.q: Which set of symptoms is classic for Ménière's disease?
choices: Episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness
Ear pain, discharge and fever after swimming
Constant imbalance for days after a viral cold
Brief vertigo on rolling over in bed and normal hearing
test.explain: Ménière's has the classic tetrad of episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Brief positional vertigo with normal hearing suggests BPPV.

test.q: How long do Ménière's vertigo episodes last under the Bárány criteria?
test.explain: The diagnostic criteria require episodes lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours.

test.q: What hearing pattern is typical of early Ménière's?
test.explain: Early Ménière's causes fluctuating low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss. A 4 kHz notch points to noise damage.

test.q: Which structure makes most of the endolymph?
test.explain: The stria vascularis secretes potassium-rich endolymph. The endolymphatic sac helps absorb it.

test.q: Why is intratympanic gentamicin used in Ménière's disease?
choices: It thins blood to improve inner ear flow
It shrinks the endolymphatic sac surgically
It kills a bacterial infection in the ear
It ablates vestibular hair cells to stop vertigo
test.explain: Gentamicin is ototoxic, especially to vestibular hair cells, so it acts as a chemical labyrinthectomy. Infection is not the cause of Ménière's.

test.q: A patient has tinnitus in one ear with asymmetric hearing loss. What is the key next test?
test.explain: Asymmetric sensorineural findings need MRI to exclude vestibular schwannoma.

test.q: Tinnitus that beats in time with the pulse most suggests:
test.explain: Pulsatile tinnitus points to vascular causes such as intracranial hypertension, venous sinus anomalies or fistulas.

test.q: Which therapy has the strongest evidence for reducing tinnitus distress?
test.explain: Guidelines recommend CBT. Supplements and routine drug therapy are not recommended for tinnitus itself.

test.q: Sudden drop attacks without loss of consciousness in late Ménière's are called:
test.explain: Tumarkin crises are thought to come from sudden otolith (utricle and saccule) stimulation in late Ménière's disease.

test.q: The buildup of excess endolymph in Ménière's is called endolymphatic ___.
test.explain: Endolymphatic hydrops is the histological hallmark of Ménière's disease.

test.q: What is the term for hearing a sound such as ringing with no external source?
test.explain: Tinnitus is a phantom sound perception.

test.q: A first-line lifestyle change for Ménière's is a low-___ diet.
test.explain: Reducing salt is the traditional first step, though the evidence for it is weak.

kidTest.q: In Ménière's disease, what happens inside the ear?
choices: The ear bone breaks in half
The tube gets too full of fluid
kidTest.explain: Too much fluid builds up in the inner ear tube.

kidTest.q: What does a Ménière's attack feel like?
kidTest.explain: Attacks cause spinning dizzy spells that can last for hours.

kidTest.q: What is tinnitus?
choices: A ringing noise in the ear
kidTest.explain: Tinnitus is hearing a sound like ringing when there is no real sound outside.

kidTest.q: What can help protect your ears?
kidTest.explain: Loud noise can damage ears and cause ringing.

kidTest.q: The inner ear helps you hear and keeps your b _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The inner ear works like a spirit level to keep you balanced.

advancedTest.q: Temporal bone studies found hydrops in all Ménière's cases but also in people without symptoms. The best conclusion is:
choices: Hydrops is a postmortem artifact of tissue processing
Hydrops reliably protects the ear against later attacks
Hydrops is a disease marker but may not be the direct cause
Hydrops is sufficient on its own to cause vertigo attacks
advancedTest.explain: Hydrops is necessary-looking but not sufficient, so it may be a marker rather than the trigger. Asymptomatic hydrops argues against it causing symptoms on its own.

advancedTest.q: A patient with Ménière's has serviceable hearing and disabling vertigo despite medication. Which next step best fits?
choices: Labyrinthectomy to remove the inner ear
advancedTest.explain: With serviceable hearing, hearing-sparing options like intratympanic steroids come first. Labyrinthectomy destroys hearing, and bilateral ablation risks oscillopsia.

advancedTest.q: Why does tinnitus loudness correlate poorly with patient distress?
choices: Limbic and attentional networks govern the emotional burden
Loudness is set by the size of the cochlear lesion alone
Audiograms measure loudness of tinnitus precisely
Distress depends mostly on middle ear pressure changes
advancedTest.explain: Distress reflects limbic and attentional processing (amygdala, cingulate), not just auditory signal strength. This is why CBT helps.

advancedTest.q: A patient has tinnitus but a normal audiogram after years of noise exposure. Which mechanism could explain this?
choices: Endolymphatic sac obstruction raising inner ear pressure
Cochlear synaptopathy cutting auditory nerve input
Vestibular hair cell ablation from an earlier infection
Otosclerosis fixing the stapes footplate in the oval window
advancedTest.explain: Loss of ribbon synapses can reduce neural input despite normal thresholds, which may drive increased central gain and tinnitus.
